questions.question: A system needs to serve 500,000 read requests per second, but a single database instance can handle at most 50,000. Which scaling approach addresses this?
questions.explanation: Read replicas distribute read query load across multiple database instances. With 10 replicas each handling 50k requests/second, you can serve 500k requests/second. Vertical scaling has limits, and write sharding doesn't help with read throughput.
options: Read replicas (multiple instances serving read traffic)

questions.question: For personalized news feeds with 100 million users, what are the main drawbacks of pre-computing and caching each user's feed?
questions.explanation: Pre-computed user caches require storing a feed for each user (100M caches), causing memory costs to explode. Additionally, when articles are updated or removed, you must invalidate millions of caches. Dynamic assembly avoids both issues.
options: Security vulnerabilities with cached user data
Memory costs grow linearly with user count
Slower read performance than dynamic assembly
Both: Memory costs grow linearly with user count AND cache invalidation becomes complex

questions.question: In a hybrid content ingestion system, a publisher's RSS feed becomes unavailable. Which fallback mechanism allows the system to continue discovering new articles from that publisher?
questions.explanation: When RSS feeds are unavailable, web scraping serves as the fallback content discovery mechanism. Scrapers visit publisher websites and extract articles directly from their HTML structure using maintained CSS selectors and site-specific patterns. It's the only option here that actually discovers new content rather than waiting or serving stale data.
options: Wait for the RSS feed to recover
Scrape new articles directly from the publisher's website
Skip this publisher until the feed returns

questions.question: When implementing category-based news feeds (Sports, Politics, Tech), which approach provides the best balance of performance and resource efficiency?
questions.explanation: In-memory filtering provides the best balance by storing complete article metadata in regional caches (like feed:US) and filtering by category when requested. This avoids the memory explosion of separate category caches (25 categories × 10 regions = 250 cache keys) while maintaining sub-200ms performance. Reading 1,000 articles from Redis takes ~10ms, and in-memory filtering adds only 1-2ms, making it much faster than real-time database queries while using significantly less memory than pre-computed category caches.
options: Store each category in separate Redis caches (feed:sports:US, feed:politics:US)
Query the database with category filters in real-time for each request
Cache complete article metadata in regional feeds and filter in-memory by category
Use machine learning to predict user category preferences dynamically

questions.question: During traffic spikes, which component typically becomes the bottleneck in read-heavy systems?
questions.explanation: In read-heavy systems, the database or cache layer typically becomes the bottleneck first because data retrieval operations are more resource-intensive than request routing or basic processing. Application servers and load balancers can usually be scaled more easily than data layers.

questions.question: Why do news aggregators implement Change Data Capture (CDC) instead of simple database polling for cache updates?
questions.explanation: CDC triggers cache updates immediately when new articles are inserted, providing sub-second freshness. Database polling would require constant queries that scale poorly, while CDC scales effortlessly and maintains real-time cache synchronization without database load.
options: Sub-second cache freshness without overwhelming the database

questions.question: Geographic data distribution reduces latency by serving content from nearby locations.
questions.explanation: Geographic distribution leverages the principle of data locality - serving content from locations physically closer to users reduces network round-trip time. This is fundamental to CDN design and regional deployment strategies for global applications.

questions.question: Why might implementing webhooks from publishers be preferred over frequent RSS polling for breaking news delivery?
questions.explanation: Webhooks provide push-based notifications that allow publishers to immediately notify the news aggregator when new content is published, reducing discovery latency from the polling interval (5-10 minutes) to seconds. This is crucial for breaking news where every minute matters. While webhooks require publisher cooperation and need fallback mechanisms, they provide the fastest possible content discovery for participating publishers.
options: Webhooks eliminate the need for any fallback mechanisms
RSS feeds are inherently less secure than webhook endpoints
Webhooks provide immediate notification when content is published, reducing discovery latency from minutes to seconds
Webhooks automatically handle content categorization better than RSS parsing

questions.question: Rank these content discovery methods from SLOWEST to FASTEST for detecting new articles:
questions.explanation: Standard RSS polling with 3-6 hour intervals is the slowest, taking hours to discover new content. High-priority polling every 5-10 minutes reduces this to minutes. Publisher webhooks provide near-instant notification (seconds) since publishers push content immediately when published.

questions.question: Eventual consistency is acceptable for news feeds where availability matters more than perfect synchronization.
questions.explanation: According to the CAP theorem, news aggregation systems often prioritize availability over strict consistency. Users prefer access to slightly outdated content rather than no content at all, making eventual consistency an appropriate choice for this use case.

questions.question: All of the following improve content freshness EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Increasing cache TTL (time-to-live) actually reduces content freshness by keeping stale data longer. The other options all improve freshness: webhooks provide immediate notifications, frequent polling discovers content faster, and CDC triggers real-time updates.

questions.question: During a major election, your Redis cache serving 100M users gets overwhelmed at 100k requests/second. What's the BEST immediate scaling solution?
questions.explanation: Read replicas are the fastest solution since each replica can handle ~100k requests/second. With just 10 replicas, you can handle 1M requests/second. Cache sharding takes longer to implement, and database queries would make the problem worse.
options: Add read replicas to distribute query load

questions.question: Match each pagination approach to its key characteristic:
questions.explanation: Offset-based pagination causes duplicates when new content shifts data. Timestamp cursors fail on timestamp collisions. Composite cursors solve this by using article ID as a tie-breaker. Monotonically increasing IDs (like ULIDs) provide the simplest solution with single ID comparisons.
right: Simplest query with single ID comparison
Causes duplicate results when new content is added
Fails when multiple articles share the same timestamp

questions.question: Cursor-based pagination prevents duplicate results when new data is added during user browsing sessions.
questions.explanation: Cursor-based pagination uses stable reference points (like timestamps or IDs) rather than offset calculations. When new data is added above the cursor position, it doesn't affect subsequent pages, eliminating the pagination drift problem common with offset-based approaches.

questions.question: Why do news aggregators like Google News download and store their own copies of publisher thumbnails rather than linking directly to publisher images?
questions.explanation: Publisher images can be slow to load, change URLs, or become unavailable, which would break the feed experience. Storing local copies ensures consistent load times and prevents broken images from disrupting the user experience across millions of daily users.
